name: Eswatini
summary: A small kingdom (formerly Swaziland), independent from Britain in 1968; one of the last absolute monarchies.

knownFor.label: Absolute monarchy
knownFor.note: The king rules with wide powers.

location.value: Southern Africa between South Africa and Mozambique; 17,364 km².

terrain.value: Mountains in the west, the middle veld and the low, dry lowveld in the east, all in a small landlocked country.

climate.value: Subtropical, with hot, wet summers and cooler, dry winters.

disasters.value: Droughts and occasional floods and storms.

urbanisation.value: Mbabane (the administrative capital) and Manzini are the main towns; most people live in rural homesteads.

disease.value: Highest HIV prevalence in the world among people aged 15–49: 27.1% (2019), according to the article.

migration.value: Some Swazi work in the mines in South Africa.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade runs through South Africa, on which the economy depends, and the Mozambican port of Maputo.

wealth.value: A lower-middle-income country with high inequality.

moneyAndTax.value: The lilangeni, pegged to the South African rand.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy, the last of its kind in Africa.

keyRulers.value: Sobhuza II (succeeded as a four-month-old after 1899; died 1982). Later and present leaders are not named here.

succession.value: The king is hereditary and has wide powers; the queen mother also holds a major role.

institutions.value: Parliament: a Senate of 30 seats and a House of Assembly of 65 seats; the article does not describe its powers.

stability.value: Pro-democracy protests from June 2021; at least 20 people were killed.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A small army and police, mainly loyal to the king.

majorWars.value: No wars in modern times; the kingdom survived the 1800s by diplomacy with the British and Boers.

territoryChange.value: The kingdom lost land to the Boers and British in the 1800s and has had its current borders since the early 1900s.

alliancesRivals.value: Member of the Southern African Development Community (SADC).

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The article gives no literacy rate; it reports school enrolment and grade completion.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads link the towns and cross the border to South Africa and Mozambique; a rail line carries goods.

religion.value: Mostly Christian, mixing with traditional beliefs.

languageWriting.value: Swazi is official along with English.

artsArchitecture.value: The annual Umhlanga (Reed Dance) and Incwala ceremonies, and traditional beehive homesteads.

socialStructure.value: The royal family, chiefs, and a majority of rural Swazi homesteads.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Swazi identity tied to the monarchy, language (siSwati) and traditional ceremonies.

dailyLife.value: Many families farm maize and keep cattle on rural land held by chiefs; maize porridge is a staple.

ideasReligions.value: Traditional rule by the king and chiefs (Tinkhundla system), with Christian faith.

colonisation.value: British high commission territory from 1903 (the article says no protectorate was established then).

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Eswatini continues as a kingdom; Swaziland was renamed Eswatini in 2018.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
